questions.q: Why is a chaos engineering finding that gets written up and then filed away without action considered worse than never running the experiment at all?
options: Because the team now has documented proof of a known weakness they chose not to fix, which is a worse position when it eventually causes a real outage
It isn't worse — documentation alone always reduces risk regardless of whether anything is fixed
Because filing the finding automatically fixes the underlying issue
Because chaos experiments are only useful for compliance paperwork
questions.explain: An unacted-on finding leaves the system exactly as vulnerable as before, but now with documented evidence the team knew and didn't act — a worse position than simple ignorance.

questions.q: A chaos experiment reveals that three service pods all share one underlying database connection pool. What is the correct response, according to this lesson?
options: Add a note to the runbook describing the shared pool as a known limitation
Ignore it, since the experiment already confirmed the system mostly worked
Rename the connection pool so it's easier to find during the next outage
Make an actual architecture change, such as giving each service its own connection pool, and track it as owned work
questions.explain: A documented caveat is a more detailed description of the same unfixed risk, not a fix — the real response is an architecture change to remove the single point of failure.

questions.q: What does "treating a finding as tracked work" actually mean in this lesson?
options: Mentioning it once in a team meeting and moving on
Filing it as a ticket with a named owner and a target date, reviewed in the same forum as error budget and postmortem action items
Assigning it to whichever engineer happens to be on call that week with no deadline
Treating it as optional work to be done only if there is spare time
questions.explain: Findings need the same accountability structure as a bug or postmortem action item — an owner and a deadline — so they compete visibly for prioritization instead of losing by default.

questions.q: How does this lesson say a team should confirm that a remediation for a chaos finding actually worked?
options: By trusting that the fix worked once the code change is merged
By asking the engineer who wrote the fix whether they are confident in it
By re-running the same original chaos experiment and confirming the steady-state hypothesis now holds
Verification isn't necessary once an architecture change has been made
questions.explain: A remediation isn't confirmed until the exact experiment that originally found the weakness is re-run and the steady-state signal holds — the same evidence-based standard used to find the problem in the first place.

questions.q: How does closing the loop on a chaos finding connect back to error budgets and production readiness reviews from earlier in this path?
options: Findings are best reviewed in the same forum that tracks error budget burn and postmortem action items, so reliability risks compete for prioritization on the record
It doesn't connect to either of them in any way
Error budgets and readiness reviews are replaced entirely once a team starts running chaos experiments
Production readiness reviews only apply to new services, never to existing ones with chaos findings
questions.explain: Treating chaos findings this way keeps them from being deprioritized informally against feature work — they compete for prioritization in the same forum as other reliability risk.
